children: By Margot Patrick and Joe Wallace
Dodgers owner Mark Walter's insurance empire made investments in an unusual way compared with peers: It invested a lot in the short term.

Around $20 billion in insurance investments at Walter's companies are under scrutiny in a federal investigation. That probe is studying how Walter-controlled insurers helped fund his other businesses, known as affiliated lending, and whether there was fraud.
The federal probe prompted Walter's insurers to conduct a review and reclassify more than a third of their assets as connected to their owner, the insurers said.

The highest concentration of affiliated lending was in short-term investments, a little-used category at most insurers. Almost all of the $5.2 billion of short-term loans Walter's insurers made last year turn out to have gone to affiliates. Walter's TWG Global conglomerate and its insurance arm have said they plan to cut most affiliated investments by the end of 2026.

Most of those billions in loans were due to mature by the end of this month. That could ratchet a funding squeeze on Walter and TWG, which recently sold a controlling stake in the Los Angeles Lakers a year after buying it.
"It's very unusual," said Alton Cogert of Strategic Asset Alliance in Washington state, who advises insurers on their investment mix.

The industry as a whole had 0.6% of its assets in short-term investments in 2024, according to an American Council of Life Insurers factbook. The category can also include some Treasury bills dated for more than three months that don't count as cash. Life insurers sometimes hold assets with maturities of under a year to help meet payouts that are about to come due.
Walter's Delaware Life had 8.6% of its overall investments in short-term loans at the end of 2025. His other main insurer, Clear Spring, had almost 14%, according to an analysis of their filings.

A spokesman for TWG Global didn't return requests for comment. In a statement on Wednesday, TWG said it "stands firmly behind the integrity of its business" and that its insurance companies invested in "real assets that are performing well." It said "there has been no fraud."

Insurers tend to buy longer-dated bonds and mortgages that pay out cash for years, matching liabilities that stretch out decades. Walter's insurers have obligations from selling annuities, a type of policy in which individuals pay upfront for retirement income later on.
Most of the short-term loans went to black-box limited-liability companies, or LLCs, with little public footprint, leaving a partial picture of what exactly Walter's insurers invested in.
Many were made through vehicles whose paperwork was filled out by representatives at four businesses. The Wall Street Journal has reported this group is a focus of the Justice Department probe.

One is Hudson Trading, based in Chicago. The firm's president registered LLCs named after places in New York state such as Dobbs Ferry, Hannacroix and Schuylerville. ?A lawyer for Hudson declined to comment.

The largest loan listed at the end of 2025 at Delaware Life was for $140 million. It came due in May. The borrower was Cypress Park Financial MP, registered in Delaware by a senior managing director at TWG, who previously worked for a Walter family office administrator.
Annual interest rates for the overall short-term lending ranged from 6% to 12%.
Walter has long done business with a network of other executives who also have owned insurance companies.
Several of the borrowers from Walter's insurers are controlled by a Dodgers co-owner, Bobby Patton, corporate filings show. The Patton companies owed around $180 million as of the end of 2025.

Personnel from ABS Capital, a Miami investment firm, set up at least nine of the LLCs that received short-term financing from Walter's insurance companies. The Journal previously reported that ABS made investments with Walter, including to buy an $85 million house in California in 2017. The investment firm was founded by two former executives at Guggenheim Partners, Walter's financial firm.
ABS Capital didn't respond to a request for comment. Patton didn't respond to a request for comment.

Short-term investments that aren't cash require insurers to hold more capital as a buffer, said Erik Miller, senior director at AM Best. When it assesses the financial health of insurers, the credit ratings company penalizes the assets compared with holdings of corporate bonds or money-market funds.

Only a few other big life-insurance groups report large holdings of short-term investments, AM Best data show. In recent years, state insurance regulators tightened rules around the investment category, after finding that some unnamed insurers rolled over loans to conceal longer-term assets.

One group reporting large short-term holdings is a set of Berkshire Hathaway life insurers, according to the AM Best data. Filings for one showed those were almost all risk-free Treasury bills that are too long-dated to count as cash.

Another group that accumulated short-term assets is Amistad Financial. The holding company owns EquiTrust, an insurer previously controlled by Guggenheim, and Heritage Life, also once operated by Guggenheim and until recently owned by Patton. Amistad acquired both of those insurance companies last year.
Short-term loans made up more than 6% of EquiTrust's assets in 2025. Many of the borrowers overlap with those at Delaware Life and Clear Spring, regulatory filings show.
Spokespeople for EquiTrust and Amistad didn't respond to requests for comment.
